This paper introduces the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model, a novel econometric framework designed for modeling and forecasting count time series. We demonstrate that the score-driven approach is ideal for tracking the evolution of time-varying parameters, offering the necessary flexibility to handle count data with complex nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks. Under mild conditions, we establish the asymptotic properties of the TV-PARX model, proving that maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) produces parameter estimates that are both strongly consistent and asymptotically normal. Monte Carlo simulations are used to assess finite-sample performance and forecasting precision. Furthermore, the practical value of the TV-PARX model's time-varying specification is illustrated through an analysis of daily new COVID-19 infections in Italy and corporate defaults in the United States. To facilitate research in this area, we have made the R package implementing the TV-PARX model accessible via CRAN at the following URL: https://github.com/giacomob/TV-PARX. This resource aims to support future studies on count time series.
Although the concept of employing stellar photometry to monitor the atmosphere for high-energy astrophysics optical experiments appears simple, achieving the high precision required to determine vertical aerosol optical depth (VAOD) to within 0.01 has been challenging. Wide-field photometry spanning various altitudes enables a rapid, calibration-independent VAOD calculation, while simultaneously serving as a valuable calibration by-product. By leveraging multi-year datasets from the FRAM (F/(Ph)otometric Robotic Atmospheric Monitor) telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory in Argentina and approximately one year of data from a comparable instrument at the future Cherenkov Telescope Array site in Chile, we have refined measurement techniques to enhance precision, potentially surpassing the 0.01 threshold. Crucially, this analysis relied on detailed laboratory assessments of the system's response to light spectrum and intensity, as the standard assumption of CCD detector linearity no longer holds under these specific observational conditions. Incorporating these careful laboratory validations into the analysis workflow has significantly improved measurement precision. These findings offer guidance for deploying similar monitors at the proposed Cherenkov Telescope Array construction site and could benefit other high-energy experiments, atmospheric科学研究, and climate monitoring initiatives that require precise cloud and aerosol observations. Notably, the methodology described here is particularly beneficial in locations where calibration air masses differ significantly from those used during standard dome calibration procedures. To facilitate future implementations, we provide a comprehensive set of analysis scripts as open source.
This study evaluates and compares numerous numerical techniques for addressing stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics, which rely on combinations of deterministic impulses, drifts, and Brownian motions. Leveraging recent work by the authors, the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion is employed to analyze sampling accuracy and quantify stepsize-dependent biases in configurational averaging. For harmonic oscillators, specific schemes yield exact configurational averaging, potentially enhancing the modeling of biomolecules where bond stretching is critical. In general systems, an optimal method is identified that exhibits significantly lower bias than alternatives. Simulations of the alanine dipeptide (both solvated and unsolvated) demonstrate that this approach achieves higher accuracy without sacrificing computational efficiency, supports larger timesteps, and maintains the conformational exploration rate. The proposed scheme represents a uniformly superior algorithm for molecular sampling, offering practical timestep increases of over 25% in vacuum and reducing errors in configurational averages by more than a factor of ten in solvated simulations at large timesteps. Ultimately, sampling accuracy emerges as a decisive element in molecular dynamics applications, influencing both scientific outcomes and practical considerations like timestep size and simulation duration. Distinct from force-field developments that prioritize spatial accuracy, this work highlights the importance of temporal sampling accuracy. In collaborative efforts where force fields are being refined, improving sampling accuracy could yield scientific benefits comparable to those of developing a new force field, while requiring minimal computational resources. Such an improvement might even replace standard practices, like lowering integration timesteps from 2.0 to 1.0 fs, with significant computational savings. As summarized by Klein et al. (J. Phys. Current automatic image description models are typically trained and assessed using crowdsourced human-generated captions, with system performance measured by similarity metrics such as BLEU, Meteor, and CIDER. Consequently, the reliability of both the systems and their evaluation hinges on the quality of these reference descriptions. As demonstrated in Section 2, existing image description datasets lack sufficient quality. I contend that more detailed guidelines are necessary, ones that balance the specific requirements of visually impaired users with the practical feasibility of generating appropriate descriptions. While high-quality data would allow for reference-based evaluation, we should also explore alternative assessment methods. These could involve analyzing which user needs are met or identifying areas for improvement, potentially through a checklist-based approach similar to that used for evaluative writing feedback (Stucke and Tabor 2015). Such a method would be particularly valuable for improving systems from low-resource starts, where collecting large volumes of high-quality data is challenging. Future research should also investigate secure mechanisms for sharing raw data among development teams, moving beyond the current limitation of sharing only evaluated results. Furthermore, we must consider how to validate systems with teams in low-resource languages that have not participated in challenge events; this could be achieved through shared tasks designed as before-and-after comparisons, akin to language evaluation frameworks (Lugger et al. 2013; Magiroiu and Luenger 2017). Finally, there is a need to develop metrics for diversity and creativity in image descriptions, ensuring that generated descriptions do not consistently focus on dominant image elements like skies or trees. By addressing these issues, we can establish more rigorous quality standards for automatic image captioning in low-resource language settings. Cognitive science offers a broad range of methodologies for creating valid and reliable assessments (Zvoch et al. 2009), and I am confident that research teams developing image descriptions for Sign Language will find these methods useful for establishing quality metrics relevant to their specific contexts and user needs. Before concluding, I wish to acknowledge two common criticisms of competitions like IWC 2020. First, some argue that competitions incentivize optimizing systems for specific evaluation metrics rather than addressing real user needs (Kulikov 2016). However, as highlighted earlier, these events have successfully raised awareness about visually impaired users in low-resource languages and facilitated collaborations between NLP researchers and cognitive science/expert teams to define context-appropriate quality standards—outcomes that would have been difficult to achieve without such gatherings. Second, there is concern that competitions attract only top-tier research teams
Quantifying complexity within quantum field theory remains a formidable challenge, primarily due to the difficulty of moving past free models and their associated Gaussian states and operations. Our approach addresses this by examining conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, offering a comprehensive analysis of complexity for both states and operators within the universal sector of their energy-momentum tensor. Central to our framework are the Euler-Arnold equations and their integro-differential extensions, which ensure the optimization problem between arbitrary states or transformations is well-defined. This work expands upon the findings detailed in arXiv:2005.02415, elaborating on the derivation techniques employed. Key areas of focus include the application of differential regularization, solving the integro-differential equation governing Fubini-Study state complexity, and investigating the underlying geometric structure. Furthermore, we derive a general expression for operator complexity, outline a numerical strategy for evaluating it, and perform specific calculations. Additional findings emerge naturally from this unified methodology.
This paper examines potential issues arising from the choice of gauge group in the bilepton model, an extension of the standard model where SU(2) is replaced by U(1)$\times$SU(2) and new bilepton bosons $X$ and $Y$ are introduced to enable three-muon decay and solve the weak neutral-current identity problem. While global properties of the gauge group are typically assumed to be irrelevant, we demonstrate that this assumption can lead to significant errors in group theory calculations and the construction of valid Lagrangians and projection operators. These findings caution against prematurely fixing the gauge group in new physics models and highlight the necessity of verifying its global properties to ensure they align with those of the product group acting on fermions. Although these conclusions were derived for the bilepton model, the implications apply broadly to similar models. Additionally, we examine whether the addition of bileptons allows for the implementation of a larger gauge group, such as SU(2)$\times$SU(2), that would act directly on fermions. Finally, we clarify misconceptions regarding the equivalence of different gauge group choices, a topic frequently debated in literature, and present a criterion for determining when groups are effectively equivalent in a specific physical context. As a byproduct of these analyses, we derive a previously absent relation between the Clebsch--Gordan coefficients used for SU(1)$\times$U(1) and those for U(1)$\times$U(1).
This paper introduces IDET systems grounded in SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM, serving as the counterparts to our optimal wideband waveforming approach detailed in [1]. We formulate optimization problems aimed at maximizing both fair-throughput and sum-throughput. Leveraging a fixed-point based alternating algorithm, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput solutions for both SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM configurations. Numerical examples are provided to outline the benefits of these new systems over traditional broadband systems and to compare their performance against the waveforming method described in [1]. Additionally, we offer guidelines for selecting the most appropriate system type based on specific application requirements. Furthermore, we contrast these choices with single-carrier waveforming options, which are deemed suboptimal for broadband scenarios. The findings indicate that IDET systems surpass single-carrier alternatives across all considered scenarios. Finally, a potential real-world implementation of this concept is discussed for smart radio environments in intelligent cities. Notably, such environments would integrate wideband sensing, sensing-informed waveforming, and dynamic radio environment management, all managed by a central entity, creating an architecture analogous to that found in intelligent car environments [2]-[4]. Such an integration would enable the creation of dynamic maps for radio coverage and channel quality alongside real-time optimization of transmitted waveforms to adhere to quality-of-service constraints. Additionally, similar to how dynamic maps of road conditions and vehicle speeds aid in navigating intelligent vehicles [2]-[4], dynamic maps of radio coverage and quality of reception could guide the selection of appropriate waveforms and modulation/coding rates to meet service-level agreements for video streaming, video conferencing, and other real-time applications [1], [5]-[7]. Such an intelligent radio environment could be established by equipping a central entity, such as a building manager, city administrator, or military commander, with a radar-like capability for sensing the environment, combined with the ability to observe and control how the environment responds to transmitted signals. Before concluding an introduction to this idea, we admit that realizing such an environment requires significant investment in infrastructure and technology, alongside careful consideration of privacy concerns regarding environmental sensing and the potential risks of misusing transmitted signals for spying or electronic spying. Fortunately, as wireless spectra continue to become scarcer and data demands grow, there is a compelling business case for exploring technologies like IDET to maximize spectrum efficiency and deliver high throughputs in broadband environments. In summary, these benefits and potential applications have been sketched out here; further research is needed

While data integration primarily involves standardizing formats, incorporating theoretical predictions is more complex due to the involvement of multiple components. Various independent groups develop distinct providers for different processes, utilizing diverse input parameters (runcards) and output structures (interpolation grids). Furthermore, because processes are measured across different scales, the PDF candidate requires DGLAP evolution, either calculated dynamically or precomputed into grids. Our goal is to automate all these steps within a single framework, making it a valuable resource for any PDF fitting group and potentially for broader phenomenological investigations. To achieve this, we have created a Python-based library called FastR (recently renamed to Sambo), which acts as a connector between runcards, prediction providers, scale setting routines, and data integration routines (which also handle error processing). This approach minimizes the customization needed from existing providers. We have developed interfaces for two dominant prediction providers: QCDlib (the foundation of CT, MM, and TW Z schemes) and Nelson grids (employed by NR and KS schemes). Additionally, we implemented a generic interface allowing other providers to be easily incorporated. Regarding scale setting, we have developed a versatile routine capable of calculating the scale from event-level data (reconstructed jets or invariant masses) or utilizing precomputed values. For data integration, we have created an efficient format-agnostic reader that loads datasets (and their errors) into vectors for optimization; it can also accommodate correlated datasets represented as matrices. To demonstrate the workflow's efficiency and flexibility, we successfully fitted a next-to-leading-order (NLO) PDF using DGLAP-precomputed grids, employing a Bayesian prior to constrain the $\gamma^*-$$J$ structure function at high $Q^2$ so it could be directly compared to nuclear PDF data. This research conducts a linear analysis of a turbulent methane-air jet flame to forecast how the reacting flow responds to upstream acoustic actuation. Within a linearized framework, capturing heat release fluctuations is essential for studying thermoacoustic instabilities and flame noise. Distinct from prior work, this study employs an active flame approach, which incorporates heat release oscillations induced by acoustic fluctuations. Implementing this approach linearly requires linearizing a combustion model; however, linearizing Large Eddy Simulation (LES) and Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) models creates closure issues, rendering them difficult to apply in this context. Conversely, Reynolds-averaged Navier Stokes (RANS) models effectively avoid these problems, making them ideal for this application. These RANS models were linearized around the mean flow characteristics of the turbulent jet flame under investigation, facilitating the analysis of thermoacoustic fluctuations. An a priori approach was used to identify the dominant modes of interaction between flow and acoustic fluctuations, which were then targeted via Bayesian inference. This study demonstrates that RANS models are well-suited for a priori analyses of thermoacoustic fluctuations and can be effectively linearized for such applications. Furthermore, the results indicate that a RANS-based Eddy Break-Up (EBU) model offers the most accurate prediction of heat release oscillations, aligning closely with fluctuations derived from LES. These findings support the use of linearized EBU models within control theories, such as RANS-backus-Goldstein (RANS-BGW) and linearized RANS-Navier-Stokes (LRNS) frameworks, for controlling thermoacoustic fluctuations. Conversely, this research confirms that LES and DNS models are unsuitable for a priori analyses regarding thermoacoustic fluctuations and pose challenges when linearized for control theory implementations. Finally, it is emphasized that RANS models remain valid only within their effective eddy turnover frequency range; thus, they may not be appropriate for analyzing high-frequency oscillations, a limitation that warrants further investigation.
Nonlocal gravity (NLG) represents a classical, nonlocal extension of Einstein's gravitational theory, modeled after the analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics in media. Within this framework, historical dependence is introduced through a constitutive relation that utilizes a causal kernel, which must ultimately be derived from observational data. This paper aims to reformulate nonlocal gravity so that the nonlocal components of the constitutive relation directly link measurable quantities, mirroring the approach found in nonlocal electrodynamics. The derived constitutive relation aligns with a recent proposal by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl [25]. Utilizing this updated constitutive relation for NLG, it is demonstrated that de Sitter spacetime does not constitute a valid solution. Furthermore, circular binary pulsar orbits are analyzed both in vacuum and when surrounded by a stellar envelope, with trajectories calculated using the NLG constitutive relation and a causal kernel formulated as a superposition of exponential decays. These results indicate that the rate of orbital period decay in a vacuum matches gravitational wave predictions from general relativity to within one standard deviation, whereas an envelope significantly accelerates this decay. Finally, the constitutive relation for NLG is compared with those in nonlocal electrodynamics and the theory of nonlocal gravity proposed by Miba and Saito.
This presentation reports on selected recent LHC findings from the ALICE, ATLAS, and CMS experiments concerning small systems. Given that the study of high-multiplicity QCD in small systems has become a rapidly expanding area of significant interest to both the heavy-ion and broader high-energy physics communities, it is not feasible to cover all related topics in this paper. Instead, the discussion will focus on measurements addressing collective phenomena in small systems and recent results on strangeness enhancement in proton-proton collisions. Readers should be aware that many other intriguing results were excluded from this discussion due to space constraints. As the field of small systems research continues to develop, future works will explore the topics omitted here. To facilitate this, we provide a comprehensive list of recent reviews on small systems research in the form of references that may be of value. Such compilations of references have proven useful for guiding the development of this research area and will prove equally valuable for training the next generation of researchers in high-energy physics. Ultimately, such reference lists serve as essential bibliographies for the future of small systems research.
The detection of certain variable X-ray sources in the Galactic Centre that have not exhibited outbursts over a ten-year monitoring period has led to the hypothesis of a substantial population of stellar-mass black holes in this area. A fundamental premise of this argument is the assertion that neutron stars in low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) do not experience long intervals between transients. However, this paper demonstrates that approximately half of the known transient LMXBs with confirmed neutron star primaries exhibit recurrence times exceeding a decade when observed with MAXI sensitivity. Furthermore, we show that to align the expected total number of neutron star LMXBs with both current observations and the galaxy's millisecond radio pulsar population, the dominant class of these systems must have recurrence times far surpassing a century for MAXI-detectable outbursts, implying that few such systems have been identified to date. Finally, we argue that future searches for transient LMXBs across a broad range of luminosities are essential to determine the actual distribution of recurrence times and to clarify the origin of millisecond pulsars. Such data would also help clarify why supermassive black hole binaries have not been observed in Galactic centre binaries after a decade of monitoring. These findings indicate that assuming uniform transient LMXB recurrence times is incorrect, and consequently, inferring populations of inactive black hole LMXBs based on non-detections during specific observation windows is flawed.
Bipartite graphs represent the connections between two separate sets of entities. These structures are frequently depicted in a two-tiered layout, where each entity set is shown as a collection of vertices aligned on one of two parallel horizontal lines, and their relationships are illustrated by edges linking corresponding vertices across the lines. A primary goal in creating such visualizations is to reduce edge crossings; however, minimizing crossings is computationally demanding and often yields drawings with so many intersections that they compromise readability. This work examines a recent method for eliminating crossings by splitting vertices, aiming to identify the minimum number of vertices that must be split to achieve a planar representation. We demonstrate that deciding whether a planar drawing is achievable by splitting at most $k$ vertices is fixed parameter tractable with respect to $k$. Furthermore, assuming the standard complexity theory of $N/(\log N)^c$, we prove that the problem is strictly $c$-hard when $k$ is defined as $a \cdot \log |V| + b$. Finally, we implement this approach and evaluate its performance on real-world datasets. Additionally, the author's portion of a companion project focuses on investigating bipartite graphs with a bi-chromatic alternating structure, seeking a circular edge drawing that avoids crossings. Such representations offer clear insights into the relationship patterns between the two entity sets. We analyze the conditions required for planar drawings exist for specific degree sequences, outlining a step-by-step algorithm to construct them, and through experiments on real-world data, we highlight instances where these alternating circular representations are feasible.
Performance degradation techniques serve as a crucial complement to side-channel attacks. This study introduces HyperDegrade, a novel method that integrates prior strategies with simultaneous multithreading (SMT) architectures. Beyond this new technique, we identify a previously unrecognized source of slowdown by analyzing cache eviction as a root cause. The resulting performance degradation is substantially greater than previous methods, thereby enhancing the time granularity available for Flush+Reload attacks. We evaluated HyperDegrade across various Intel microarchitectures, achieving significant slowdowns that, in specific microbenchmark scenarios, represent a three-order-of-magnitude improvement over state-of-the-art solutions. To assess the effectiveness of performance degradation in amplifying side channels, we introduced and validated specific leakage metrics. Our findings indicate that HyperDegrade improves time granularity without compromising trace quality. Furthermore, we conducted a fair comparison of three performance degradation strategies when paired with Flush+Reload from an attacker's viewpoint. We also devised an attack targeting an underutilized vulnerability in OpenSSL, where HyperDegrade demonstrated superior performance by reducing the number of required Flush+Reload traces needed for success by a factor of three. In terms of cryptographic contributions, we revisited the recently proposed Raccoon attack on TLS-DH key exchanges, extending its application to other protocols. Leveraging HyperDegrade, we constructed an end-to-end attack proving that Raccoon-like exploits can succeed with real data, addressing a gap left by earlier research. As a direct consequence of this demonstration, major vendors have already initiated efforts to mitigate this attack vector; we discuss these developments in detail. Finally, we explored the potential of HyperDegrade as a physical performance tuner, offering practical recommendations for system designers and computer scientists regarding the risks associated with such attacks. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/CacheSideChannel/HyperDegrade.
An unknotting operation represents a local modification applied to knot diagrams. It is possible to convert any knot diagram into a trivial unknot diagram through a combination of unknotting operations and Reidemeister moves. These operations hold substantial significance in knot theory, particularly for analyzing knot complexity and invariants. Furthermore, they play a crucial role in fields such as biology, chemistry, and physics, where they help investigate the complex entanglements found in strings, organic molecules, and DNA. This paper introduces a novel unknotting operation known as the diagonal move, applicable to both classical and welded knots. We demonstrate that the crossing change, Delta-move, Sharp-move, Gamma-move, n-gon move, pass move, and 4-move can all be achieved via sequences of diagonal moves. Additionally, we define a distance metric based on the diagonal move and examine its characteristics. Finally, we calculate the diagonal move distance between various classical and welded knots. As part of this analysis, we compare this distance with that associated with the Delta-move. To facilitate this study, we also developed Python scripts that automate the computation of diagonal move distances. These scripts are available at the following GitHub link: https://github.com/wunkt/DiagonalMove.
Coordination serves as a vital capability in multi-agent systems, enabling the completion of objectives that single agents cannot achieve alone. This study examines how a team of strategic agents selects among multiple tasks within a stochastic framework, specifically focusing on two tasks with randomly distributed and partially observable difficulties. We demonstrate that when prior distributions regarding task difficulty are diffuse, a Nash equilibrium with a straightforward, intuitive linear structure emerges. Conversely, we find that if the prior distribution is not diffuse, an agent's best response to an affine strategy profile may become nonlinear. Furthermore, we present an algorithm capable of efficiently calculating a data-driven Nash equilibrium restricted to the class of affine policies. Finally, we propose a practical method for implementing a data-driven affine Nash equilibrium policy in real-time scenarios.
This paper demonstrates the embedding of regularly acting groups and diagonal groups into wreath products under their product action by utilizing Cartesian Decomposition. Additionally, the explicit construction of this decomposition is applied to construct a regularly acting group that cannot be embedded into a direct product of two copies of its own acting part. Finally, a comparable construction is employed to create a group that is diagonal under its acting decomposition, yet fails to embed into the acting component of its wreath product decomposition.
The high-frequency sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors is constrained by quantum shot noise and ultimately by optical losses within the signal-recycling cavity. This limitation represents a primary barrier to detecting gravitational waves from binary neutron star mergers in both current and future detectors, as it remains independent of arm length and the level of injected squeezing. In this study, we propose a sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, derived from a Michelson interferometer by optically linking the end mirrors to form an additional cavity. This configuration creates a triply-coupled cavity system capable of surpassing the loss-induced high-frequency limit inherent to signal-recycled Michelson interferometers. Using parameters comparable to advanced LIGO+, a sloshing-Sagnac design could achieve sevenfold improved sensitivity at 2.5 kHz, or a fourfold increase in signal-to-noise ratio for typical post-merger binary neutron star waveforms. As an evolution of the Michelson architecture, the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer offers a viable topology for upgrading current detectors and for future-generation observatories.

Extra-large scale massive multiple-input multiple-output (XL-MIMO) systems represent a promising solution for delivering ultra-high data rates in environments with high user density. Because the physical dimensions of XL-MIMO arrays are comparable to the distances separating them from user equipments (UEs), the system experiences spatial non-stationarities and distinct visibility regions (VRs). These factors, combined with high UE density and limited pilot resources, make the design of random access (RA) protocols and scheduling algorithms particularly difficult. This paper introduces a joint RA and scheduling approach called the non-overlapping VR XL-MIMO (NOVR-XL) protocol. This method leverages the unique VRs of individual UEs to enhance RA performance and prioritizes scheduling UEs with non-overlapping VRs within the same payload data pilot resource. Simulation results demonstrate that this proposed scheme yields substantial improvements in sum rate compared to conventional RA methods, while also lowering access latency and overall connectivity performance. Additionally, simulations confirm that the NOVR-XL system exhibits robustness against errors in angle of arrival (AoA) and angle of departure (AoD) estimations. Despite these performance gains, the findings indicate that the actual array dimensions are a critical element for realizing the benefits of extra-large scale massive MIMO in ultra-dense deployment scenarios.

Although neural language models have largely replaced traditional $N$-gram models due to superior performance, our findings suggest that $N$-grams still yield satisfactory results in many scenarios, effectively capturing significant linguistic knowledge at a low computational cost. Leveraging this insight, we propose training a neural model to predict the residuals between a selected $N$-gram model and the actual data distribution. This hybrid approach enables the neural component to concentrate on deeper linguistic understanding while offering a flexible framework for adapting to different $N$-gram choices without altering the model's architecture. Experiments across three standard tasks—language modeling, machine translation, and summarization—demonstrate that this method consistently matches or surpasses existing state-of-the-art solutions. Furthermore, our approach requires minimal extra training time during adaptation and facilitates easy comparison between different $N$-gram configurations, facilitating straightforward optimization toward specific goals. Our implementation is accessible via [github.com/srshw/ResN].
This study investigates the performance of Informed OCR (iOCR), a system developed to correct errors in conventional OCR for vote tabulation using a spell correction algorithm. The findings indicate that iOCR outperforms traditional OCR methods. Notably, when processing texts with high error rates from conventional OCR, iOCR reduced error rates by 83.33% compared to an 18.33% reduction for standard methods. Additionally, the research concludes that deep learning-based error correction algorithms are more effective than hybrid approaches for this task. The source code for the proposed algorithm is accessible at https://github.com/Deepak-1997/informed-ocr. Image text recognition has become a vital component of many applications, yet conventional OCR systems often struggle with accuracy, particularly when handling non-standard written forms. To address this, this paper proposes a deep learning-based error correction algorithm designed to improve recognition results for incorrect text generated by conventional OCR. Building upon recent advances in sequence-to-sequence deep learning models, our approach utilizes a combination of convolutional, recurrent, and attention mechanisms. Extensive experiments conducted on multiple public datasets, including our own collected data, demonstrate that the proposed method significantly surpasses conventional OCR systems in accuracy. Furthermore, the system achieves high accuracy even on data sets for which conventional methods have reached saturation.
This study investigates potential global atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere using a simplified General Circulation Model (GCM) derived from the University of Hamburg's Portable University Model for the Atmosphere. The model incorporates simplified linear boundary layer friction, Newtonian cooling, and dry convective adjustment. Through a series of controlled experiments, researchers varied the planetary rotation rate and the imposed equator-to-pole temperature gradient. These variables were converted into dimensionless parameters to define a parameter space where distinct circulation regimes are identified and categorized. Significant trends emerge when altering the planetary rotation rate alongside frictional and thermal relaxation timescales. The progression of circulation regimes with respect to planetary rotation closely mirrors findings from laboratory studies on rotating, stratified fluids, particularly when topographic $\beta$-effects are included to simulate planetary vorticity gradients caused by spherical curvature. Additionally, a regular baroclinic wave regime appears at intermediate thermal Rossby numbers, with its characteristics and dominant zonal wavenumber heavily influenced by radiative and frictional damping strengths. These regular waves display notable similarities to baroclinic storms observed on Mars under specific conditions. At the highest rotation rates, multiple jets develop when the Rossby deformation radius and other eddy-related scales are significantly smaller than the planetary radius; these resemble the multiple zonal jets found on gas giant planets. These jets form on scales comparable to the most energetic eddies, poleward of the supercritical latitude, near the Rhines scale. Finally, the balance of heat transport between eddies and zonally symmetric flows varies significantly with rotation rate ($\Omega$), weakening as rotation accelerates. At lower rotation rates, eddies dominate heat transport, whereas zonally symmetric flows take over at higher rotation rates. This shift occurs because eddy viscosity scales positively with $\Omega$, while zonal flow efficiency improves as inertial damping increases relative to frictional damping under stronger rotation. These discoveries from this simplified GCM offer insights applicable to planetary science, meteorology, and fluid dynamics, potentially guiding future climate modeling efforts. Notably, topographic $\beta$-effects play a crucial role in determining zonal flow velocities and eccentricity, warranting their inclusion in future climate models, especially on planets with curved surfaces like Mars and Earth.
This study presents a real integral formulation for the reciprocal $\Gamma$ function using a regularized hypersingular integral. It confirms the equivalence between this new form and the standard complex representation, subsequently deriving a regularized complex expression that follows the conventional Hankel contour. The work also establishes identities connecting this regularized complex form with other known representations. Finally, the authors derive a series definition for the Gamma function's reciprocal along the same Hankel contour, ultimately Pochhammer-extending this series representation to the entire complex plane. These approaches offer a novel framework for investigating the Gamma function and its reciprocal. Additionally, this paper serves as a continuation of the research detailed in [1].

Hydrodynamic theories provide effective strategies for simulating the complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems that are otherwise computationally challenging. In this study, we develop a novel stochastic hydrodynamic method within the positive-P phase-space framework specifically for interacting Bose gases. Among the most critical hyperparameters for neural networks, the loss function plays a pivotal role, yet selecting the appropriate one remains challenging due to the vast array of available options. Despite this, related studies often fail to provide rigorous justifications for their specific choices, suggesting a dogmatic approach within the deep learning community that lacks empirical grounding. This work investigates supervised classification tasks to evaluate how loss function selection influences training outcomes. Although some functions yield suboptimal results, our empirical analysis demonstrates that underutilized losses, such as KL Divergence, can significantly surpass state-of-the-art alternatives. These findings underscore the necessity of treating the loss function as a tunable hyperparameter rather than adopting it as a fixed default. To facilitate this, we introduce a unified framework for comparing diverse losses, which is implemented via a accessible Python library also available for R and Python. Additionally, we document a comprehensive survey of 27 common loss functions used in deep neural networks. Our codebase and detailed guidelines aim to guide researchers in effectively integrating this framework into their workflows to optimize classification performance. Ultimately, our results indicate that performance metrics beyond accuracy, such as the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUROC), offer a more equitable assessment when different loss functions are compared. By making this framework easily adoptable, we anticipate that our work will streamline workflow optimization and serve as a valuable reference for future studies. Notably, our framework supports not only standard losses but also custom-defined losses, allowing for flexible evaluation of emerging options. To ensure reproducibility, we also provide default recommendations for classification workflows across two widely adopted datasets.

Cardiac auscultation serves as a critical point-of-care technique for the early identification of heart conditions, yet the automatic analysis of heart sounds for detecting abnormalities is hindered by additive noise and sensor-specific degradation. This study proposes methods to tackle cardiac abnormality detection in the presence of both distortion types. Initially, we mathematically evaluate the impact of additive and convolutional noise on short-term filterbank features and Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) layers. Guided by this analysis, we introduce a hybrid approach combining linear and logarithmic spectrogram-image features. These 2D representations are fed into a Residual CNN (ResNet) for detecting heart sound anomalies. Validation was conducted using an open-access dataset of noisy heart sounds recorded by various stethoscope sensors. The proposed method outperforms conventional techniques, achieving an AUC of 91.36%, an F-1 score of 84.09%, and a Macc of 85.18%. Furthermore, the approach demonstrates superior mean accuracy across diverse source domains, including variations in stethoscope types and noise levels, confirming its robustness under different recording conditions. By effectively mitigating the effects of background noise and sensor variability in phonocardiogram (PCG) classification, this combination of linear and logarithmic features with a ResNet classifier facilitates the development of computer-aided cardiac auscultation systems capable of operating in noisy environments using low-cost stethoscopes. This capability supports the early diagnosis of heart diseases through the automatic identification of pathological sounds. Furthermore, it enables telemedicine solutions for cardiac auscultation in resource-limited areas via cloud-based platforms accessible through simple devices like smartphones and laptops. Notably, during this research, the network was trained using Chisolp et al.'s dataset [1], which comprises PCGs from a single source domain recorded with one specific stethoscope type under varying noise levels. Future work will explore datasets covering multiple source domains, characterized by diverse stethoscope types, noise conditions, and geographic locations. Additionally, this research aligns with the emerging field of sound source separation, aiming to extract physiological signals from noisy PCGs without relying on target-domain specific training data as required in conventional source separation methods. Regarding the evaluation of linear and nonlinear features under corrupted conditions, this study utilizes the Tino et al. dataset [2], a multi-source domain collection of finger-print sounds exposed to different levels of additive noise. Furthermore, this work does not depend on deep convolutional networks for feature extraction
Gas temperatures in star-forming galaxies typically fall within the 20–30 K range, a range where the excitation of low-J molecular lines, particularly isotopologues like $^{3}$$\nu$C, is often in the non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (non-LTE) regime. Consequently, line emissions arise from different thermal components of the molecular gas, rendering single-component non-LTE fitting inadequate for precise temperature measurements. Although multi-component non-LTE fitting has proven effective for abundant lines like CO, its application to rarer isotopologues and higher-order transitions is often constrained by a lack of detectable transitions across various transitions and isotopologues. Furthermore, derived component temperatures can exhibit significant uncertainty. This study introduces a Bayesian inference framework to estimate molecular gas temperatures ($T_{\rm mol}$) without relying on multi-component non-LTE line fitting. We applied this framework to multi-transition observations of the $^{3}$$\nu$A, $^{3}$$\nu$C, and N$_{2}$$\nu$$^{+}$ transitions in the W3OH star-forming region and the IRAS 08339$-$4554ULLULCG. The results indicate that previous estimates of $T_{\rm mol}$ in these sources via multi-component non-LTE fitting may be biased too high, as our method derives significantly lower temperatures: 18$^{+20}_{-8}$K for W3OH, 16$^{+14}_{-6}$K for IRAS 08339, and 20$^{+17}_{-7}$K for the host galaxy of the ULLULCG. These findings underscore the necessity of non-LTE inference over simple non-LTE fitting when exploring fainter molecular transitions and isotopologues to fully characterize the molecular gas. Our approach serves as a valuable tool for rapidly assessing plausable $T_{\rm mol}$ values across larger samples of star-forming galaxies and LULULCGs, thereby guiding the selection of appropriate transitions for mapping spatial distributions of the molecular gas.
We demonstrate that for ASEP with step initial conditions and a second-class particle originating at zero, the particle's velocity converges almost surely to a uniform distribution on $[-1,1]$ as time approaches infinity. This result affirmatively settles Conjectures 1.9 and 1.10 from [Amir, Angel and Valko, "The TASEP speed process", Annals of Probability 39, 1205--1242, 2011] and enables the construction of the ASEP speed process. Additionally, we establish that ASEP behaves hyperdeterministically along deterministic spacetime cones, a property we utilize to define a martingale associated with the speeds of second-class particles within these cones. Finally, by applying optional stopping to this martingale at a conical exit time, we recover the distribution of speeds at that specific time.
This study examines various mathematical models developed during the current pandemic to tackle key public health concerns regarding epidemic dynamics and their origins. We begin by outlining the fundamental characteristics of the classic Kermack-McKendrick models before exploring their generalizations and applications to contact networks, viral co-circulation, epidemic curve trajectories, probability distributions, and passage times required to define compartments in these models. Collectively, these examples underscore that a system of differential equations designed for a specific epidemiological challenge relies fundamentally on the epidemiological, medical, and biological context driving its formulation and analysis. Merely fitting differential models to data without considering biological feasibility may yield statistically significant results but will ultimately fail to offer actionable insights for managing, mitigating, or controlling the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic. To guide future modeling efforts, we propose ten principles for constructing meaningful and useful epidemiological models and conclude with several recommended areas for further research. By reviewing common misconceptions found in recent literature, we aim to clarify these basics and enhance the quality of future epidemiological modeling related to SARS-CoV-2 and potential viral variants. Additionally, this survey serves as an introductory resource for mathematicians entering the field of epidemiology. The complete set of ten principles is available at: https://www.mathematicalepidemiologyblog.com/2020/09/coronavirus-videos-nine-principles.html.
It remains uncertain if bulge expansion causes the flattening of the star-forming main sequence (MS) at high masses. To examine how bulges influence the MS, we analyzed the NUV$-r$ color—a reliable tracer of specific star formation rate—in the central ($r<R_{50}$) versus outer regions of 6,401 local star-forming galaxies. Our results show that for galaxies with $M_{\ast}<10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, the central NUV$-r$ is only about 0.25 magnitudes redder than the outer regions. However, above $M_{\ast}=10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, the central NUV$-r$ becomes significantly redder than the outer regions, indicating that bulges in massive galaxies are more evolved. When sorting galaxies by S\'ersic index $n$, those with $n$>2.0 exhibit redder central NUV$-r$ colors than those with $n$<2.0, even when controlling for B/T ratio and $M_{\ast}$. This implies that bulge star formation depends more strongly on $n$ (or central mass density) than on the B/T ratio. Furthermore, the fraction of galaxies with $n$>2.0 rises sharply with mass for $M_{\ast}>10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, aligning with the turnover in the MS at this transition mass. We conclude that the growing proportion of low specific star formation rate, dense bulges in galaxies with $M_{\ast}>10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, rather than an increase in B/T, drives the flattening of the $M_{\ast}$$-$SFR relation at high masses. This supports the hypothesis that the $n$ in the S\'ersic fitting law better isolifies specific star formation in bulges than the B/T ratio. To further validate $n$ as a superior tracer, we developed a new four-component (bulge/disk/bar/spiral arm) fitting algorithm capable of resolving these structural components in individual galaxies.
This research conducts a cross-lingual sentiment analysis of news articles by applying zero-shot and few-shot learning techniques. The objective is to categorize Croatian news into positive, negative, and neutral sentiments using a Slovene dataset. The proposed system utilizes a trilingual BERT-based model trained on English, Slovene, and Croatian. The study evaluates various configurations using two-language datasets and introduces a straightforward multi-task model for sentiment classification. Assessments are carried out across single-task and multi-task experiments within both few-shot and zero-shot scenarios for Croatian and Slovene. Findings indicate that the trilingual BERT model outperforms other models in single-task experiments. Furthermore, the model achieves superior results in multi-task experiments compared to previous approaches, with notable improvements observed during few-shot evaluations. The model also performs well in zero-shot experiments within a multi-task setup. These outcomes demonstrate that leveraging pre-trained language models like BERT, along with multi-task learning and shared embedding layers, is effective for sentiment classification in low-resource languages such as Croatian and Slovene. By utilizing the TBBSD dataset, this research offers a significant contribution to sentiment analysis in Croatian through a novel approach. The dataset and model are accessible at: https://github.com/JulijaG/cs_sentiment.
This study reports the potential detection of a nonmonotonic radial rotation profile in a low-mass, low-luminosity giant star. While low- and intermediate-mass stars typically exhibit rigid rotation on the main sequence, stellar evolution into the giant phase—characterized by core contraction and envelope expansion—generally predicts a profile with a rapidly rotating core and a slower envelope and surface. KIC 9267654, however, displays a surface rotation rate exceeding that of its bulk envelope, contradicting standard angular momentum conservation expectations. We enhance the spectroscopic constraints on the surface rotation, confirm that pulsation frequencies align with previously determined core and envelope rotation rates, and establish that the star lacks significant chemical peculiarities. Furthermore, we evaluate evidence against the presence of a tidally interacting companion. Finally, we explore possible origins for this anomalous rotation profile, such as the accretion of a giant planet or anomalous angular momentum transport via tidal inertial waves driven by a close substellar companion, and advocate for additional observational and theoretical investigations.
Fake news spreads rapidly across social media, reaching global audiences and endangering communities. While deep learning models perform well on labeled data for specific events, their efficacy often drops when encountering new events due to domain shifts. This creates a significant hurdle for existing detection systems when dealing with emergent events where large, labeled datasets are scarce. Furthermore, adapting to new events typically requires training a model from scratch or extensive fine-tuning, which is often costly, impractical, and difficult to sustain in real-world scenarios. To overcome these limitations, we introduce MetaFEND, an end-to-end framework designed to rapidly learn fake news detection for emerging events using only a small number of verified posts. By combining meta-learning with neural process methods, our approach leverages the strengths of both techniques. Specifically, we incorporate a label embedding module and a hard attention mechanism to better manage categorical data and filter out irrelevant content. Extensive experiments on multimedia datasets from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate that MetaFEND effectively detects fake news in previously unseen events, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, the framework's ability to quickly incorporate new data into training is verified through a simulated online continuous learning process. Golay complementary matrices (GCM) have recently attracted significant attention due to their potential applications in omnidirectional precoding. In this paper, we extend GCMs to multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays (GCA) and introduce new construction methods for GCA pairs and quads. These constructions are enabled by a set of identities defined over a commutative ring. We demonstrate that a quaternary GCA pair is feasible when the product of array sizes across all dimensions equals a quaternary Golay number, subject to an additional constraint on the factorization of that product. Regarding binary GCM quads, we conjecture that feasible sizes can be arbitrary and verify this for dimensions up to 78×78 and other sparsely distributed sizes. For quaternary GCM quads, we show that all positive integers up to 1000 can serve as the size for a single dimension. Finally, we outline potential uses of GCA quads in improving omnidirectional precoding systems. In the simplest configuration, a quaternary GCM quad with an N×N matrix size is shown to reduce sidelobes by a factor of N compared to a single Dirichlet complementary matrix, provided the matrices form a valid quad. Furthermore, GNRCA arrays are applicable in systems utilizing N orthogonal pilot sequences for omnidirectional pilot transmission, where N represents the product of the array sizes in each dimension. Notably, GNRCAs offer a significant advantage over complementary code sets: for a set size of 100, a quaternary GCA quad allows total sizes of 10,000, 100,000, 1,000,000, or 10,000,000 matrices, whereas a quaternary set is limited to exactly 100 matrices. Beyond this example, our construction methods for GCA pairs and quads facilitate flexible solutions for large sets. Additionally, we establish that quaternary GCM quads are feasible in any dimension greater than or equal to two, and we propose a construction for quaternary GCA pairs in a single dimension (feasible up to 1000) that could potentially be adapted for two dimensions.
Laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT) represents a new minimally invasive approach for ablating intracranial structures to manage mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE). Automating lesion quantification through pre- and post-treatment region of interest (ROI) segmentation offers an objective means to evaluate therapeutic efficacy. While deep learning methods, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), represent the current standard for ROI segmentation, they depend heavily on extensive annotated datasets, which are difficult to gather for emerging procedures like LITT. To address this limitation, we introduce a Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis Framework (PAVAE) designed to increase both the volume and variety of training data. This framework comprises two sequential networks: a mask synthesis network and a mask-guided lesion synthesis network. To leverage extrinsic information for enhanced supervision, we developed a condition embedding block (CEB) and a condition embedding block with mask (CEB-M). These components were integrated into an intrinsic loss function alongside a mask loss, a pixel loss, and a gradient loss. Our results indicate that a hybrid approach combining intrinsic and extrinsic losses yields superior lesion synthesis quality compared to using intrinsic losses alone. Furthermore, a generative model trained on augmented datasets demonstrated improved segmentation accuracy. Ultimately, this study presents a straightforward yet effective methodology for increasing dataset diversity and volume to enhance lesion segmentation performance. The source code for this framework is accessible at https://github.com/PhuocNguyen1997/PAVAE.

Although large language models (LLMs) achieve human-level performance across many natural language tasks, it remains unclear whether they absorb knowledge more effectively from structured sources like knowledge graphs (KGs) or from unstructured text. This study introduces a technique to embed structured knowledge into LLMs by directly training T5 models on factual triples extracted from knowledge graphs. When applied to the smaller WikiMovies dataset, our method achieved a threefold increase in exact match scores on the MetaQA task relative to the T5 baseline. A key benefit of this approach is that it eliminates the need for aligning knowledge graphs with text corpora during data preparation, rendering it especially advantageous for industry-scale knowledge graphs. Additionally, because the method relies solely on factual triples, it remains agnostic to the specific schema of the knowledge graph. Finally, the influence of the non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter on both the shadow radius and thermal profiles is further explored.

The analysis utilizes a data set with an integrated luminosity of 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ from $pp$ collisions recorded by LHCb at center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV. The measured branching fractions are given by:
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{B}(B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0) &=
(4.3\pm0.5(\text{stat})\pm0.3(\text{syst})\pm0.3(\text{frag})\pm0.6(\text{norm}))\times10^{-4},\\
\mathcal{B}(B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0) &=
(2.8\pm1.0(\text{stat})\pm0.3(\text{syst})\pm0.2(\text{frag})\pm0.4(\text{norm}))\times10^{-4},
\end{align*}
where the uncertainties arise from statistical precision, systematic effects, and two external inputs: the $f_s/f_d$ ratio and the branching fraction of the $B^0\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ calibration channel. Generally, constructing the submodule lattice $L(M)$ for a specific module $M$ poses significant challenges. While R. P. Stanley proposed in \cite{St} a technique to build a distributive lattice from its join irreducibles, determining all such irreducible submodules remains a difficult undertaking. For multiplicity-free modules $M$, we introduce an adaptation of Stanley's approach grounded in the composition factors of $M$. This method requires a collection of submodules $A_1,\ldots , A_n$ with known lattice structures that encompass all of $M$'s composition factors, enabling the reconstruction of $L(M)$. We demonstrate this procedure for a series of Verma modules $M(\gl_n)$, where $n$ is a positive integer, associated with the Lie superalgebra $\osp(3,2)$. Our results indicate that for $n\ge 2$, the lattice $L(M(\gl_n))$ is isomorphic to the (extended) free distributive lattice of rank 3. Additionally, we discuss the applicability of this construction to other multiplicity-free modules. As an illustration, we determine the exact lattice structure for a particular module $M_0$ identified by S. Donkin as having an unknown submodule structure; we find that $L(M_0)$ is isomorphic to the product lattice $J_1\times J_2$, where $J_1$ and $J_2$ represent the pentatomic and squaretic distributive lattices, respectively. Building on the construction detailed in this article, we also propose an algorithm implemented in Maple designed to determine the submodule lattice for various Verma modules corresponding to simple Lie superalgebras. Furthermore, we outline potential applications of determining submodule lattices for multiplicity-free modules within the study of simple Lie superalgeras.
This study demonstrates that certain well-established recurrent operators—specifically the recurrent curvature, Ricci, Jacobi, shape, and Weyl operators—play a crucial role in determining whether biharmonic hypersurfaces are minimal within Euclidean space. Additionally, the authors introduce a new operator, the $\mathcal{R}^\star$-recurrence, and examine its significance. They define a class of hypersurfaces in Euclidean space whose curvature operator exhibits $\mathcal{R}^\star$-recurrence, commonly referred to as $\mathcal{R}^\star$-Hypersurfaces, and investigate their properties to derive several notable results. Furthermore, the work addresses the problem of classifying such $\mathcal{R}^\star$-Hypersurfaces that constitute biharmonic graphs over minimal minimal submanifolds in Euclidean space. Finally, the authors consider biharmonic $\mathcal{R}^\star$-Hypersurfaces embedded in Euclidean space that satisfy specific conditions, aiming to determine their explicit formulation. The research holds geometric significance and may find applications in related fields of physics and mathematics, particularly concerning the geometry of submanifolds in Euclidean space. Furthermore, the introduced concepts and methods could be valuable for geometric analysis on Riemannian manifolds. In the broader context of recast geometry, this work aligns with efforts to define similar concepts on manifolds, as seen in the geometric analysis conducted on Lorentzian manifolds by A. O. Baruen, A. C. Baruen, and X. Zhao (2019).
For any rational number $p/q$, numeration in base $p/q$ is defined by a function mapping finite words over the alphabet $A_p=\{0,1,...,p-1\}$ to rational values. The image of this function is denoted by $N_{p/q}$. While $N_{p/q}$ encompasses all nonnegative integers, existing literature typically concentrates on the subset of words evaluating to these integers; this set forms a chaotic, non-context-free language. In contrast, this work examines subsets of $(N_{p/q})^d$ that are $p/q$-recognisable, meaning they can be recognized by finite automata operating over $(A_p)^d$. First, we provide a characterization of these sets as those definable within a specific first-order logic, drawing a parallel to the B\"uchi-Bruy\`ere Theorem for integer-based numeration systems. Second, we demonstrate that neither the natural ordering relation nor the modulo-$q$ operator are $p/q$-recognisable. Finally, we derive a characterization of diagonal sets in $(N_{p/q})^d$ that are computably enumerable, showing that such sets admit algorithms comparable to those used in integer numeration systems. To support these findings, we introduce an automatic structure for the diagonal sets of $(N_{p/q})^d$ that operates similarly to the structure found in integer-based systems.

This decay is identified via the subsequent decays $D_s^{*-}\rightarrow D_s^{-}\gamma$ and $D_s^{-}\rightarrow K^-K^+\pi^-$. The extracted differential decay rate is analyzed using the Caprini-Lellouch-Neubert (CLN) and Boyd-Grinstein-Lebed (BGL) parametrisations to determine the corresponding form factor quantities. From the integrated differential decay rate, the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^+\nu_{\mu}$ branching fraction is determined to be ${\mathcal{B}}(B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^+\nu_{\mu})=(7.92\pm0.34\pm0.26\pm0.16)\%$, where the uncertainties correspond to statistical significance, experimental systematics, form factor extraction, and production fractions, respectively. The derived quantity $|b_{B_s}\times f_{B_s}|$ is also calculated and compared against theoretical predictions. Furthermore, the differential decay rate for $B^0_d\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^+\nu_{\mu}$ is measured, although its branching fraction cannot be determined due to lack of significant data. Finally, the ratio of branching fractions ${\mathcal{B}}(B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^+\nu_{\mu})/{\mathcal{B}}(B_s^0\rightarrow D_{s}^{-}\mu^{\+}\nu_{\mu})$ is calculated and contrasted with theoretical expectations.
This study tackles the persistent challenge of extracting dynamical information from noisy acoustic emission signals generated by an adhesive tape being peeled under a constant traction velocity. By applying a phase space reconstruction method, we confirm deterministic chaotic dynamics through the identification of a correlation dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent within a specific range of traction speeds. These findings are interpreted using a model that underscores the deterministic nature of acoustic emissions by linking them to stick-slip dynamics. Notably, the correlation dimension and Lyapunov exponent vanish beyond the chaotic regime, where events become stochastic and characterized by a higher information dimension. These conclusions are further supported by analyses of average recurrence plots and recurrence rate curves. Ultimately, these findings offer valuable insights for characterizing non-Gaussian stochastic processes. The work presented here extends our previous research detailed in "Quantification of Chaotic Dynamics in Simple Nonlinear Stochastic Processes" by S. Lesiewicki and J. S. Albert, which introduced a similar phase space reconstruction approach to analyze a nonlinear damped stochastic process [1].
In the early 1930s, K. Menger explored the concept of an abstract angle function, defining it broadly for metric and semi-metric spaces. He also formulated two challenges regarding the conformal embeddability of spaces equipped with an angle function into Euclidean spaces. Although these problems garnered attention later, solutions were limited to specific instances of metric spaces. This article updates the definition of the angle function to accommodate a broader class of spaces characterized by a betweenness relation, which we consider a more natural framework. Within this generalized setting, we resolve both problems originally posed by Menger. Furthermore, we establish that for metric spaces, the betweenness relation and the conformal embeddability of the associated angle function into Euclidean spaces are equivalent concepts. Neural network-based point cloud models have achieved significant success and are extensively utilized in safety-critical domains, including Lidar recognition systems for autonomous vehicles. This paper introduces TPC, a transformation-specific smoothing framework that delivers tight and scalable robustness guarantees for point cloud models against such attacks. We begin by classifying common 3D transformations into three groups: additive (e.g., shearing), composable (e.g., rotation), and indirectly composable (e.g., tapering), offering generic robustness certification strategies for each category. Subsequently, we define specialized certification protocols for various specific semantic transformations and their combinations. Extensive experiments on multiple common 3D transformations demonstrate that TPC significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art methods; for instance, our framework increases certified accuracy against twisting transformations along the z-axis (within 20°) from 20.3% to 83.8%. This paper presents an explicit formulation of the weight component of Serre's conjecture for GL_2, grounded in Kummer theory and deliberately avoiding p-adic Hodge theory. Fiber-reinforced composites featuring nanofiller-modified polymer matrices hold significant promise for enhancing the safety of high-risk engineering structures. The results demonstrate that this new method can accurately reconstruct multiple through-holes with radii as small as 1.19 mm and delaminations resulting from low-velocity impacts. These findings indicate that integrating piezoresistivity with conductivity-based spatial imaging and physics-based inversion strategies can enable precise damage shape reconstruction in self-sensing composite structures. Such capability could transform condition monitoring and damage detection, ultimately improving the safety of safety-critical applications.

We introduce a tensor framework for Euclidean spaces that prioritizes geometric vectors, validating this method by establishing several integral identities involving vector integrands. We demonstrate that if a right-angled Artin group $A(\Gamma)$ admits a non-trivial, minimal action on a tree $T$ that is not a line, then $\Gamma$ must contain a separating subgraph $\Lambda$ for which $A(\Lambda)$ stabilizes an edge in $T$. Advancements in technology have enabled big data processing, yet this has created substantial computational challenges when solving large-scale linear systems or performing matrix inversions. Consequently, there has been significant research into fast, approximate iterative methods for matrix inversion accelerated by Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), offering viable alternatives where traditional direct inversion methods are too costly. Existing techniques include the Neumann Series (NS), Newton iteration (NI), Chebyshev Iteration (CI), and Successive Over-Relaxation. This study introduces a novel iterative algorithm derived from the NS, termed "Nested Neumann" (NN). This approach generalizes higher-order iterations of NI and CI by leveraging a computationally efficient iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, dependent on a specified "inception depth." Mathematical analysis confirms that the NN method: (i) converges provided the preconditioning matrix satisfies the spectral norm condition required for NS, (ii) achieves a convergence rate equivalent to an order of (inception depth plus one), and (iii) performs optimally with an inception depth of one or two, contingent upon available RAM. Additionally, we derive an explicit formula for NN suitable for massive sparse matrices, accounting for increased computational costs. Crucially, we establish an analytical equivalence between NS and NN (including NI, CI, and higher orders), a finding particularly relevant for mMIMO systems. Finally, the NN method is applicable to positive semi-definite matrices for inversion and can be utilized for any linear system, whether sparse, non-sparse, or complex. Performance metrics indicate that NN significantly surpasses direct inversion methods (NI, CI, NI-3, and NS) in speed while delivering comparable accuracy. The source code for this new method is accessible at https://github.com/robertroberts900/ApproximateMatrixInversion. Furthermore, considering limited radio frequency (RF) chain resources, our analysis demonstrates that nested averaging of MMSE detection and filtering (NI + NS), enabling real-time operation in massive multi-user systems with many access points, is significantly faster and equally accurate as a single NS inversion. Similarly, for real-time real-time beamforming and system training, the combination of NS and NN (NN + NS) is significantly quicker than using two NS inversions, while maintaining identical accuracy. Ultimately, the NN method represents a significant contribution to mathematics, engineering, computer science, and related fields. Notably, this research was conducted during a lockdown to support large-scale contact tracing initiatives for pandemic management.
Contextual linear bandits represent a theoretically significant model with extensive practical utility, recently attracting considerable attention in wireless applications where communication constraints often limit performance, particularly when contexts exist in a high-dimensional $d$-dimensional space. This paper addresses a distributed memoryless contextual linear bandit learning scenario where agents observe contexts and select actions, yet are geographically separated from the central learner who performs the optimization without direct access to the contexts. Assuming contexts follow a specific distribution, we introduce a method requiring approximately $5d$ bits per context when the distribution is unknown, and zero bits per context if it is known. This approach achieves a regret bound nearly identical to that of a fully observable setting. Specifically, the bound for the unknown distribution case improves upon existing results by a $\log(T)$ factor (where $T$ is the time horizon), while the bound for the known distribution case reaches information-theoretic tightness. Numerical experiments using a circular team team formation protocol confirm that the proposed algorithm effectively scales even with small increases in the number of teams. These findings suggest that light-weight coding schemes can significantly enhance performance in distributed contextual learning, especially when contexts are high-dimensional and communication resources are scarce. Furthermore, these results offer advantages over extreme learning deep reinforcement learning methods, which demand substantial resources and are difficult to deploy in message-passing networks with numerous nodes.
